title: Redwood x Clearwave — Security & Privacy Review

Agreement to share SOC 2 report, KMS integration guide, and schedule a short on-prem/private deployment architect call.

transcript:
Header:
- Date/Time: 2026-06-10 11:00 AM PT
- Duration: ~53 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jon Rivera (Redwood SE), Alina Gomez (Redwood CSM); Sarah Long (Clearwave CISO), Mark Chen (Cloud Architect), Priya Desai (Eng Manager), Tom Ellis (Legal)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
- Quick intro, then scope to discuss data handling and privacy, retention, PII/PHI, KMS and 'no training' guarantee.

00:00:12 Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll give a quick overview then jump into the security questions. folks who we should call out?
00:00:22 Sarah Long: hi Sarah here, I'm head of security at Clearwave, and Mark is cloud lead, Priya is eng. looking to make sure any model service meets our PHI requirements and SOC two controls.
00:00:33 Maya Patel: great, thanks. jon and i will handle the technical bits; jon, feel free to jump in.
00:00:39 Jon Rivera: yep, hi all. agenda — retention, encryption/KMS, access controls, audit logs, and confirmation around training on customer data.

00:01:05 Mark Chen: first question — by default what does Redwood store? do you retain prompts and responses? for how long? and can we disable retention?
00:01:18 Jon Rivera: good question. short answer: for our hosted product, we retain request and response logs for billing, debugging and quality monitoring. default retention is 30 days, with a 90-day option for enterprise. however for Dedicated and Private deployments you can opt out of retention for customer-visible content; logs can be configured to only keep metadata or to export directly to your S3. we also support a policy to expire prompts immediately if required.
00:01:49 Sarah Long: when you say 'we retain' — is that used to train models? we cannot have PHI used to improve models.
00:01:56 Maya Patel: absolutely — Redwood has a formal policy: we do not use customer prompt/response content to train our public models. content stored for debugging or analytics is never used to update model weights. for hosted customers who opt-in to feedback, that's explicitly opt-in and documented, but enterprise accounts under contract can disable all content retention.
00:02:18 Tom Ellis: do you have that in writing? we need contractual language for 'no training on customer data'.
00:02:24 Maya Patel: yes, we have standard data-use clauses and we can add a specific 'no training' rider or addendum; i'll include the specific language in the security packet.

00:03:05 Priya Desai: and what about PII/PHI redaction or detection? is there an out-of-the-box filter?
00:03:13 Jon Rivera: we provide optional PII detection tooling and a content-moderation pipeline you can plug in pre-ingest. for Private/Dedicated you can run our redaction layer in your VPC so sensitive fields never leave your environment. there's also a schema enforcement API if you want to restrict types of inputs.
00:03:30 Priya Desai: ok, that helps. is there any automatic tokenization or masking? sometimes devs accidentally log whole transcripts.
00:03:38 Jon Rivera: we recommend client-side tokenization and masking for the highest assurance; we also have server-side filters that can mask common PHI patterns. but best practice for PHI is to use Private deployment or dedicated hosting with customer-managed keys.

00:04:12 Mark Chen: speaking of keys, what's your KMS story? can we bring our own keys? rotate keys? use HSM?
00:04:21 Jon Rivera: yes — we support customer-managed keys via AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and Azure Key Vault for hosted customers. for Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS over a secure link; for Private (VPC/on-prem) you can use an HSM and keep keys entirely in your environment. key rotation is supported and we log key usage. i'll send the KMS integration guide after the call.
00:04:41 Sarah Long: is data encrypted at-rest and in-transit? any field-level encryption?
00:04:46 Maya Patel: all data is TLS in transit. at rest we encrypt using AES-256. field-level encryption is available via envelope encryption patterns with customer-managed keys — again we'll share the implementation notes.

00:05:33 Mark Chen: audit logs — what do you capture and can we export to our SIEM? we need immutable logs for audit purposes.
00:05:41 Jon Rivera: Redwood provides detailed audit trails: auth events, API calls, model version used, request metadata (IP, user-agent), and admin actions from the console. logs are tamper-evident and can be exported in near real-time to S3, CloudWatch, or a syslog endpoint for SIEM ingestion. retention length configurable per contract.
00:06:02 Sarah Long: do you include request/response content in audit logs by default? we do not want the content in our SIEM; only metadata is fine for us.
00:06:10 Jon Rivera: default export can exclude request/response bodies; we can configure exports to only include headers/metadata and a request_id to tie back to data stored in Redwood if you have an auditor-approved process.

00:07:05 Priya Desai: for RBAC and SSO — can we do SAML-based SSO? SCIM provisioning for user sync?
00:07:12 Maya Patel: yes, we support SAML 2.0 and OIDC for SSO with SSO enforced on the account. SCIM provisioning is available for enterprise customers to automate user lifecycle. roles support least privilege — admin, dev, billing, read-only, etc.
00:07:32 Mark Chen: do you provide fine-grained roles for model rollout and access to logs? e.g., devs can call APIs but only ops can see raw transcripts.
00:07:41 Jon Rivera: yes we have route-level permissions and per-resource RBAC. you can separate ability to create/deploy model endpoints from ability to view or export content.

00:08:25 Sarah Long: on compliance — SOC 2? ISO? any pen tests?
00:08:32 Maya Patel: Redwood completed SOC 2 Type II in 2025; ISO 27001 certification is in progress with expected completion this year. we also do annual third-party pen tests and internal red-team exercises. i'll attach SOC2 report and high-level pen test summary.
00:08:51 Tom Ellis: and data residency — we operate globally, but PHI needs to stay in US regions. do you have region-level hosting and private deployments?
00:09:00 Jon Rivera: yes — hosted API can be region-scoped for data residency (US, EU, APAC depending on availability). for strict residency or compliance we recommend Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) where all data and control plane components reside in your network.
00:09:20 Mark Chen: if we go Dedicated, will the logs and raw prompts be isolated to our tenancy?
00:09:26 Maya Patel: Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools and tenancy-level separation; logs and storage are separated and we can set retention policies at the tenant level or stream logs to your account.

00:10:05 Priya Desai: regulatory question — we handle PHI under HIPAA. does Redwood sign a BAA?
00:10:13 Maya Patel: yes, we have BAA templates for customers handling PHI. we'll include the BAA draft in the packet. for Private on-prem deployments, the control plane can be customer-managed which aligns well with HIPAA.

00:12:40 Mark Chen: curious about telemetry — what operational telemetry do you collect from clients for performance tuning, and is that tied to content?
00:12:48 Jon Rivera: we collect anonymized usage metrics (latency, token counts, error rates) for product health. operational telemetry is separate from request content by default. any PII/PHI attributes are not part of the telemetry namespace; if you need, we can provide a PI-restricted telemetry stream.

00:14:10 Sarah Long: the "no training" vs "used for quality" line can be fuzzy. can you explain exactly what is happening when a hosted customer reports an issue and sends us logs?
00:14:23 Maya Patel: absolutely — the default flow: logs are accessible to your admins for debugging; our SRE team can access logs under a strict access control and only when necessary for support. support access is audited and requires justification. none of that content is used to update public models. for aggregate product improvement we may compute metrics (e.g., top error classes) but that is aggregated and stripped of customer identifiers. any explicit model training on customer data requires an explicit opt-in and contractual agreement.
00:14:56 Tom Ellis: we'll want explicit contract language.
00:15:00 Maya Patel: understood — we will provide the clause and can add an addendum if needed.

00:18:00 Priya Desai: operationally, for Private deployment do you push updates or do we manage upgrades?
00:18:07 Jon Rivera: for Private we offer two modes: customer-managed (we provide artifacts and you run upgrades) or Redwood-managed where we orchestrate updates into your environment subject to a change window. both options are supported and patching can be done via your control plane.

00:20:30 Mark Chen: can you demo how audit logs look? sample fields?
00:20:35 Jon Rivera: yes — we'll include sample log schema in the packet; key fields are timestamp, event_type, actor_id, resource_id, request_id, model_id, model_version, latency_ms, status_code. request and response bodies are optional and configurable.

00:24:12 Sarah Long: cross-tenant data leakage — any mitigations?
00:24:18 Jon Rivera: strict tenant isolation at the storage layer, network segmentation, and model instance isolation. we also run tenancy-aware memory zeroing for KV caches between sessions. note transcriptions: sometimes engineering notes will refer to 'KV cash' or mis-typed terms in our docs — but the isolation is real — we can show architecture diagrams.

00:27:05 Priya Desai: are there limits on exporting large volumes of logs? we may want full archive for 7 years.
00:27:12 Maya Patel: we can stream all logs to your archival bucket for indefinite retention; pricing varies. archival exports are common for compliance.

00:31:00 Mark Chen: legal will want encryption key custody details and proofs for key rotations. can you provide KMS audit logs?
00:31:07 Jon Rivera: yes — KMS usage logs can be exported from your cloud provider and we correlate them with our access logs. for on-prem HSMs you control the key lifecycle.

00:35:10 Sarah Long: last technical question — are model weights ever stored in a shared cache that could persist customer data?
00:35:18 Jon Rivera: model weights are immutable artifacts; any inference caching is on request-level KV caches that we can isolate per-tenant. we do not write prompts back into model weights.

00:38:45 Tom Ellis: action on legal — we'll need the BAA and the 'no training' clause and a statement on breach response timelines.
00:38:55 Maya Patel: noted — we'll include breach notification SLA and contact path.

00:45:00 Alina Gomez: quick recap — maya will send SOC2 and BAA draft; jon sends KMS guide and sample log schema; alina will coordinate the private deployment architecture call; customer to send required SIEM fields.
00:45:20 Sarah Long: that works. thank you.
00:45:33 Maya Patel: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the packet today and target the architecture call for next week.
00:45:42 Priya Desai: thanks all.
00:45:50 Meeting ended.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-heard acronyms (SOC two vs SOC 2), speaker labels may jump, and some technical terms like "KV cache" were transcribed as "K-V cash".
